clue.text: Newspaper's a steal, one to replace ft?

indicators.note: to replace says one thing is swapped in for another: the letter for one takes the place of the last two letters named

parts.note: as a noun, a steal is an act of stealing, which is a theft
the two letters f and t as printed, the pair that gets taken out
one, written as a Roman numeral, is I

explanation.surface: A newspaper so cheap it is practically a giveaway might take the place of the Financial Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to replace' swaps the FT ending THEFT for I, the Roman one. The surface's 'a steal' is a bargain and FT the Financial Times, a rival British paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An example by name: a British daily launched in 2010 as a cheap, compact sister title of The Independent.

clue.text: White wine bottles dad ordered for the fish

indicators.note: to bottle something is to hold it inside, so the wine goes around the other letters

parts.note: hock is the British name for German white wine from the Rhine

indicators.note: ordered here means put into a new order, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, its three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Dad has asked for bottles of white wine to go with the fish course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' is not a restaurant order but a call to put dad's letters in a new order, and 'bottles' is a verb, wrapping the wine around the result.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a North Atlantic relative of the cod, the staple of British fish and chips.

clue.text: Gershwin is inspirational to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means only part of the word before it is wanted, a run of neighbouring letters

explanation.surface: An admirer remarks that the composer Gershwin is fairly inspiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to some extent' takes three consecutive letters from inside 'inspirational'. Most solvers think first of George Gershwin; this is his brother, the lyricist.
explanation.definitionFit: An example by surname: the lyricist brother of composer George Gershwin had this first name.

clue.text: Conduct of senior politician responsible for publicity?

indicators.note: a politician responsible for a department is named after it, so the publicity word comes first, like a job title

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a piece of publicity
a minister is a senior member of a government, in charge of a department

explanation.surface: The behaviour of a top politician whose brief is the government's image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'responsible for' works like a job title: as the Health Minister runs health, whoever runs publicity would be the AD MINISTER. 'Conduct' looks like a noun, behaviour, but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as verbs: to conduct an inquiry or a survey is to manage and run it.

clue.text: Summer is more dismal when there's no sun

indicators.note: when there's no says the thing named next is absent, so its letter is dropped from the word before

parts.note: sadder is the comparative of sad, meaning more dismal or gloomy

explanation.surface: The warm season feels gloomier when the sunshine fails to appear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when there's no' removes S from SADDER. 'Summer' is not the season: read it as sum-mer, one who sums.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword-only sense: a 'summer' is one that sums, a person or machine doing addition.

clue.text: Lady sounding bubbly

indicators.note: sounding says the answer is heard in the name of the fizzy drink rather than spelt the same way

parts.note: bubbly is slang for champagne, and Mumm is a famous champagne house

explanation.surface: A woman comes across as lively and effervescent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounding' means the answer is heard in Mumm, a famous champagne or 'bubbly'. 'Lady' is the form of address: servants once said 'Yes, mum', a clipped ma'am.
explanation.definitionFit: A form of address: servants once said 'Yes, mum' to the woman of the house, a clipped version of ma'am.

clue.text: Fine fellow at home continued to sit up for sweet Fanny Adams

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the whole string of pieces is read from the bottom to the top

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads
F is the abbreviation for Fellow, as in FRS, Fellow of the Royal Society
someone who is at home is in
to have sat on is to have stayed seated, as a committee sat on into the evening

explanation.surface: A decent chap stayed in, sitting up late to wait for a sweet girl called Fanny Adams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reads the whole string FFINSATON from the bottom of this down entry. 'Sweet Fanny Adams' is British slang for nothing at all, a polite stand-in for a ruder phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for nothing whatsoever: the definition is a euphemism (sweet FA), and the answer means no hint or chance of something.

clue.text: Rather declare briefly? OK

definitions.note: OK is the brief, two-letter postal form of Oklahoma, and what is wanted is the nickname of that place

parts.note: sooner means rather, as in 'I would sooner walk'
to state something is to declare it formally

explanation.surface: Someone asked whether they would prefer to keep their announcement short simply agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'OK' looks like a throwaway word of agreement; it is the definition. Said 'briefly', OK is Oklahoma's postal abbreviation, and that state is nicknamed after the 'Sooners', settlers who claimed land early.
explanation.definitionFit: A nickname: OK is the short postal code for Oklahoma, named for the 'Sooners' who grabbed land before the official 1889 opening.

clue.text: A middle east office is to move abroad, leaving gulf

indicators.note: leaving says the letter for the last word departs from the word for moving abroad

parts.note: to emigrate is to leave your own country and settle in another
G is an abbreviation for Gulf, as printed on maps

explanation.surface: A firm's Middle Eastern branch is relocating overseas and quitting the Gulf region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' takes G out of EMIGRATE. The 'office' is not a building: it is the rank or post held by an emir.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: it is the rank, post or territory of an emir, a Muslim ruler in the region.

clue.text: Women aboard dread flying in a Lear?

indicators.note: aboard means on board or inside, so the letter for women goes within the letters that follow
flying suggests letters thrown up in the air and landing in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, its five letters rearranged
W is the abbreviation for women, as on changing-room doors and clothing sizes

explanation.surface: Female passengers are terrified of flying in a Learjet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying' rearranges DREAD into EDARD and 'aboard' puts W inside it. The surface suggests a Learjet; the Lear meant is the Victorian writer of nonsense verse, one example of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: An example by first name: the nonsense poet who wrote 'The Owl and the Pussycat' was Edward Lear.

clue.text: Swift's tome cried out, deism principally trashed

indicators.note: out can mean astray or not in the right place, so the letters before it are put into disorder
trashed means thrown away, so the letter picked from the word deism is discarded

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange
taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: principally means chiefly or first of all, pointing at the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A book by Jonathan Swift protested loudly and rubbished the basics of deism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principally' picks D from deism, 'trashed' throws it out of TOME CRIED, and 'out' rearranges the remaining TOMECRIE. Swift looks like the author of Gulliver's Travels but is just the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as adjectives: a meteoric rise is a very rapid one, as fast as a shooting star.

clue.text: Secondary posters intended to reach cooler staff

parts.note: for can mean bound for or meant to arrive at, as in the train for London
cooler is slang for prison, and warders are the British name for the guards who work there

explanation.surface: Less important wall notices are aimed at the more fashionable employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posters' are people who post mail, not wall notices, and those who post it a second time send it on. 'Cooler' is slang for prison, whose staff in Britain are warders.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: people who send letters on to a new address post them a second time, after the original sender.

clue.text: Ultimately Oscar Wilde wasn't wicked, bent maybe

indicators.note: wicked suggests misbehaving, so the letters before it do not stay in their proper order
ultimately means at the very end, pointing at the final letter of the word after it

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange
taken as written without its apostrophe, part of the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A verdict on Oscar Wilde: not evil in the end, though perhaps a little crooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' gives the R ending Oscar and 'wicked' rearranges it with WILDE WASNT. Bent is a stiff wiry grass, and 'maybe' marks it as one example of a dry grass stalk.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: bent is a stiff wiry grass, and the answer is a thin dry stalk of such grass.

clue.text: Pop on the coach comes from blasted trannie

indicators.note: blasted means blown apart, so the letters of the word after it are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, its seven letters rearranged; a trannie is British slang for a transistor radio

explanation.surface: Pop music on the bus is blaring out of a wretched transistor radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blasted' rearranges TRANNIE, British slang for a transistor radio. 'Pop' is the verb, to hop on, and the coach is a railway carriage, not a bus.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the answer means to board a train, and a coach is a railway carriage you might pop onto.

clue.text: Look in a thesaurus for this old character

indicators.note: look in is an instruction to search inside the long word that follows for a run of letters

explanation.surface: Advice to consult a book of synonyms to find an archaic letter or symbol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look in' asks for consecutive letters inside 'thesaurus'. 'Character' suggests a letter of an old alphabet; it is a person, a figure from the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a figure from the Old Testament book of Genesis, Jacob's hairy twin who sold his birthright.

clue.text: Medical check is most poor

definitions.meaning: an examination by a doctor, here one done on the body's surface to look for allergies or TB
the superlative of skint, British slang for having no money, read as a single word

explanation.surface: A health examination turns out to be of the lowest quality.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is read as one word, the superlative of skint, which is British slang for penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: One is a real allergy or TB procedure; the other, run together, is the superlative of British slang for penniless.

clue.text: Caught boring formerly favoured TV presenter in the club

parts.note: ex means former or formerly, as in an ex-wife

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into, so the letter for caught goes inside the letters that follow

parts.note: pet as an adjective means favourite or favoured, as in a pet project
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
Ant McPartlin is a British TV presenter, half of the duo Ant and Dec

explanation.surface: Someone is found tediously lecturing a once-popular television host at the clubhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' drills the cricket abbreviation into the three-part run that follows it. 'In the club' is British slang for pregnant, and the presenter is half of the duo Ant and Dec.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean pregnant: 'in the club' is British slang, short for 'in the pudding club', and an expectant mother is awaiting a baby.

clue.text: Barker for example embraced by hairy Sid is put out

indicators.note: embraced by means held within, so the Barker name sits inside the rearranged letters
hairy is slang for wild and risky, so the letters of the word after it are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written, its three letters rearranged
Sue Barker is a British former tennis champion and TV sports presenter, one example of a Sue

explanation.surface: A noisy dog, say, is miffed at being hugged by a shaggy man called Sid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hairy' disarranges Sid's letters into ISD and 'embraced by' wraps them round the first name. Barker is no dog: the surface hides a British tennis champion turned TV presenter behind a capital at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as past participles: a statement put out by the press office has been published or released.

clue.text: Career girl's left work

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl; the 's only joins it to what follows
op is short for opus, a numbered musical work

explanation.surface: A woman devoted to her profession has walked out of her job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career girl' reads as one phrase, but the clue splits between the two words: career is a verb, to rush headlong.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as verbs: to career downhill is to rush along at full speed, like a horse at its fastest pace.

clue.text: Expert to probe some chaos

indicators.note: to probe is to push into, so the expert word goes inside the word for some

parts.note: any can stand for some, as in 'have you any money?'
arch as an adjective means very experienced or expert, as in an arch criminal

explanation.surface: A specialist is to investigate a certain amount of disorder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to probe' pushes ARCH into ANY. Expert is an adjective here: arch can mean very experienced, as in an arch criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both name a state of lawless disorder with nobody in control.

clue.text: Bond has a following surprisingly in palace? Not half!

parts.note: ff is the abbreviation for 'and the following pages' in references

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests an unexpected arrangement, so the letters after it are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: not half means only half of the word before it is used, here the back half

explanation.surface: James Bond turns out to have plenty of fans inside Buckingham Palace, and how!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' keeps only ACE from palace, and 'surprisingly' rearranges IN ACE into IANCE. 'Not half!' is also a British exclamation meaning 'very much so', which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym as a noun: an archaic word for a pledge of faith, especially a marriage contract, which is a binding tie.

clue.text: See you check always before beginning to invest offshore

indicators.note: before places the first two pieces ahead of the letters picked from the last two words

parts.note: ch is the chess notation abbreviation for check
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

indicators.note: beginning to points at the opening letter of each of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: Advice to make sure you always do your checks before you start putting money overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to' takes the opening letters of both 'invest' and 'offshore', and 'before' sets the other two pieces ahead of them. 'See you' looks like 'make sure you' but is the goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both are informal ways of saying goodbye, the answer being the breezy British one.

clue.text: German workers getting day off

indicators.note: off says the letter for day is taken away from the word for workers

parts.note: hands are manual workers, as in farm hands or all hands on deck

explanation.surface: Employees in Germany are being given a day's holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' takes D out of HANDS. 'German' defines by example: a common first name for a German man, their form of John.
explanation.definitionFit: An example by name: a common first name for a man in Germany, short for Johannes, their equivalent of John.

clue.text: Opinion in Tory right: Miliband's respected

indicators.note: in places the opinion word between the two pieces given by the next two words

parts.note: a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party, abbreviated Con
a side is a point of view in a dispute, as in hearing both sides
Ed Miliband led Britain's Labour Party from 2010 to 2015; the 's is only a possessive

explanation.surface: On the right wing of the Conservative Party, the view is that the Labour leader is well regarded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' drops the opinion word between the pieces from 'Tory' and 'right', which the surface fuses into one faction, the Tory right. The Miliband wanted is the Labour leader of the day, known by his short first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of esteemed, as in a highly considered scholar, one who is well thought of.

clue.text: British actor seen in clubs

definitions.meaning: Jeremy, the English star of Brideshead Revisited who won an Oscar for Reversal of Fortune, known here by his surname
golf clubs with angled metal heads, as opposed to woods

explanation.surface: An English film star is spotted in nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions: the surname of the actor Jeremy, and the metal-headed clubs in a golf bag rather than nightclubs.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the Oscar-winning Jeremy is also the name for the metal-headed clubs in a golf bag.

clue.text: Us gangster stole, a case for Chicago police

parts.note: a stole is a long scarf or shawl worn over the shoulders

indicators.note: the case of something is its outer covering, so only the first and last letters of the two-word phrase are kept

explanation.surface: An American mobster committed a theft, giving the Chicago police something to investigate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case for' keeps only the first and last letters of 'Chicago police', and 'stole' is the garment, not the verb. The definition is the nickname of Chicago mob boss Al Capone.
explanation.definitionFit: A nickname: Al Capone, the Chicago mob boss of the Prohibition years, was known by it.

clue.text: Lamb is partly stewed

indicators.note: partly means only a part of the next word is used, a run of its inner letters

explanation.surface: The lamb in the pot is only half cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' takes three consecutive letters from the middle of 'stewed'. The definition is loose: a young female sheep is called a ewe lamb.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose example: a female lamb is called a ewe lamb, though strictly the word means an adult female sheep.

clue.text: Bachelor leaving disturbs rest

indicators.note: leaving says the letter for bachelor departs from the word for disturbs

parts.note: bothers means disturbs or troubles, as in the noise bothers me
B is the abbreviation for Bachelor in degrees such as BA and BSc

explanation.surface: A single man's departure wakes everyone who was sleeping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' takes B out of BOTHERS. 'rest' is not sleep: it is the remainder of a group.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as nouns: the rest of a group are the remaining people, everyone apart from those already mentioned.

clue.text: Bears mess endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means without its end, so the final letter of the word for mess is dropped

parts.note: a hash is a mess or muddle, as in making a hash of things

explanation.surface: Big furry animals keep making a mess without ever stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the final H of HASH. 'Bears' is a verb, not the animals: one who bears a scar or a grudge possesses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as verbs: someone who bears a scar, a title or a grudge possesses or carries it.

clue.text: "Spectator" sees witney represented

indicators.note: read as re-presented, presented again in a different form, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange
taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange; Witney is a town in Oxfordshire

explanation.surface: A political magazine watches the Oxfordshire town of Witney being spoken for in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' is read as re-presented, rearranging SEES WITNEY. The Spectator is a British political weekly and Witney an Oxfordshire town, then the Prime Minister's constituency.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both are someone who watches an event happen and can describe what they saw.

clue.text: A lot of money returned in this period

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word for a lot of money is read from right to left

parts.note: pots, as in pots of money, is informal for a large amount of cash

explanation.surface: A large sum was paid back during this stretch of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reads POTS backwards. 'Period' is not a span of time but the American name for the punctuation mark that ends a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym across the Atlantic: period is the American word for the dot ending a sentence, the British full stop.
